children: CMO, Tilaknagar Industries, on creating brand experiences that move beyond reach to build cultural relevance, consumer memory and lasting brand equity

Ahmed Rahimtoola, CMO of Tilaknagar Industries, brings over 25 years of experience across marketing, advertising and business development, with a career spanning brands and organisations including United Breweries, Reliance ADAG and Allied Blenders & Distillers. With deep expertise in branding, consumer marketing, advertising and new product development, he has played a key role in shaping and revitalising some of India’s well known alco-bev brands.

In this exclusive interview, Ahmed Rahimtoola discusses what it takes to turn brand experiences into lasting cultural memory, how brands can move beyond visibility to build distinctiveness, and why consumer behaviour; not just reach, must ultimately define experiential success. He also shares his perspective on Tilaknagar Industries’ evolving House of Brands strategy, the cultural role of Mansion House, the next chapter for Imperial Blue, and how innovation and entertainment can create relevance in a regulated category.
What metric tells you an experience has created memory, not just reach?
Reach tells you that you have been seen. Memory tells you that you have been remembered and ideally, that the consumer has started doing something with what you gave them.

We look at a combination of signals: spontaneous brand association, consideration, trial, repeat engagement, the conversations an idea creates, and ultimately, whether these translate into business outcomes. There is also a simple test I find valuable: does the idea continue to live when the media spend stops?

Our journey with Mansion House is a good example. We have consistently worked to move brandy from being viewed as functional and occasion-specific to something more social, contemporary and culturally relevant. A Warm Welcome, Mansion House Boyzzzz and #DadInEveryMan were different expressions of that same brand-building journey.

With Imperial Blue, the starting point is different. Men Will Be Men has already created enormous cultural memory. The opportunity is to understand which elements of that equity remain powerful and build the next chapter without diluting what made the brand distinctive.
Ultimately, the strongest evidence of memory is when consumers remember the idea and the feeling, not just the advertisement. And that memory must eventually translate into business.
What role does culture play in shaping your brand experiences?
Culture gives a brand permission to be part of people's lives but that permission has to be earned.
Our starting point is not, “What cultural moment can we attach ourselves to?” It is, “What is already true about this brand and its consumers that gives us a legitimate role in culture?”

Mansion House, for instance, has been deeply embedded in South Indian culture and cinema over decades. Our role has been to understand what that relationship means to consumers and make the brand contemporary without losing its authenticity.

That led us to the territory of warmth: connection, inclusivity and making people feel welcome. From there, we could explore friendship, humour and social connection through different formats, including Mansion House Boyzzzz. We also recognise that India is not culturally homogeneous. A national brand can have a common ambition while still needing to understand very local codes, occasions and sensibilities.

Culture, therefore, isn't about chasing trends. It is about finding the intersection between what is true to the brand, relevant to consumers and distinctive enough for the brand to contribute meaningfully.
What makes an experience memorable enough to stay with the consumer?
I think three things need to come together: a human truth, a distinctive expression and something worth talking about.
People rarely remember advertising because every product feature was communicated perfectly. They remember something because it made them feel something or gave them a story they wanted to share.
That is why we have increasingly moved beyond thinking only in terms of campaigns to thinking about stories, platforms and experiences.

Mansion House Boyzzzz, for example, used friendship, humour and everyday situations to create a branded entertainment property. It gave a legacy category a contemporary voice and allowed the brand to participate in popular culture rather than simply advertise around it.

Similarly, Welcome The Now used music, regional talent and inter-generational friendships to create a world around the Flandy proposition. The objective isn't to make every communication entertaining. It is to create something consumers would want to spend time with even if the brand wasn't asking them to.
How do you know when an activation is building the brand versus merely creating visibility?
The simplest test is: if I remove the logo, can you still tell which brand it belongs to? Visibility can be purchased. Distinctiveness has to be built.

Before we invest in an activation, we ask what piece of brand equity it is strengthening. Is it reinforcing a distinctive territory? Is it changing the perception we want to change? Is it creating an association consumers should own?

For Mansion House, the ambition has been to broaden the role of brandy from functional to social, and from occasional to culturally relevant. That requires more than individual campaigns; it requires consistent work across innovation, storytelling, entertainment, digital and consumer experiences.

Imperial Blue presents a different challenge. It already has an enormous recall. The task is to protect and strengthen the distinctive memory structures consumers associate with the brand while finding new ways to keep it culturally relevant. The question isn't whether an activation generated impressions. It is whether the brand is more distinctive, relevant and valuable after it than it was before.
How do you measure whether an experience has actually changed brand perception?
We start by defining the perception we want to change and then measure against it through brand association, consideration, trial, engagement and, over time, behaviour.

But perception change is rarely the result of one campaign. It is usually cumulative. With Mansion House, for example, the objective has been to broaden how consumers think about both the brand and the category. That has required sustained investment across innovation, communication and consumer engagement.
So, we look at both short-term response and long-term movement. The real proof is when a perception stops being a campaign message and becomes an established consumer association.
What consumer behaviour are you trying to change through experience, not just communication?

We want to broaden the occasions and contexts in which consumers engage with the category. That means moving beyond a purely functional or occasion-specific role and creating relevance around socialising, friendship, entertainment and contemporary lifestyles.

Flandy is a good example. The proposition and Welcome The Now campaign brought new energy, music and regional culture into the category. You cannot advertise your way into a new behaviour. You must give people a reason to experience the category differently.
In a regulated category, where can experience do what advertising cannot?

A regulated category forces you to think beyond conventional advertising, and I see that as a creative advantage. It pushes us toward entertainment, culture, partnerships, creators and experiences that people actively choose to engage with.

Advertising can tell consumers what a brand stands for. Experience allows you to demonstrate it. Importantly, this isn't about finding ways around regulation. It is about building brands responsibly within it by creating genuine consumer value.
With consumers increasingly engaging with brands through culture and entertainment, how do you decide which cultural moments are worth a brand investing in and which are just noise?

The first question isn't, “How many people are watching?” It is, “Why does our brand have a right to be here?” We look at four things: Is there a genuine cultural shift? Is it relevant to our consumer? Does the brand have a credible role to play? And can we contribute something distinctive rather than simply add another logo to the conversation?

That is why we increasingly see entertainment as more than a media vehicle. We can create our own stories, characters and formats, or participate in existing cultural platforms where the brand has a genuine role. Mansion House Boyzzzz was a deliberate example. Rather than create another short-form advertising campaign, we built a branded entertainment property around humour, friendship and local storytelling to help modernise perceptions of brandy.

Welcome The Now took a different route, using music, regional artists, influencers and an original anthem to build a cultural property around Mansion House Flandy. The temptation today is to chase the moment. We would rather create a point of view that can outlive the moment.
Data can tell us where attention is moving, but it cannot always tell us whether a brand should enter that conversation. That requires judgement.
As Tilaknagar expands beyond its traditional brandy base, how do you ensure each new category earns its own consumer relevance rather than simply adding to the portfolio?
Our ambition is not to build a portfolio where every brand sounds like Tilaknagar. It is to build a portfolio where every brand has a reason to exist.

Every category has a different consumer, occasion, competitive environment and cultural code. We therefore don't believe in taking what worked for Mansion House and simply putting a different label on it.

What we can carry across is a deeper understanding of the Indian consumer and an ability to identify opportunities where a category or brand can be made more relevant. You can see that in the way we are building the portfolio. Flandy brings innovation and new occasions into brandy. Monarch Legacy Edition takes us into luxury. Seven Islands allows us to participate in premium whisky. And Imperial Blue gives us an iconic whisky brand with significant existing consumer equity and cultural memory.

Imperial Blue is particularly interesting because it demonstrates the importance of respecting what already works. Men Will Be Men has created enormous recall over decades. We don't need Imperial Blue to become Mansion House. We need to understand what makes Imperial Blue distinctive and build its next chapter from there.
Our ambition is to build a House of Brands, where each brand plays a different role while together creating a stronger and more diversified spirits business.
Scale is important, but distinctiveness is what will make that scale sustainable.
Ojasvita Trivedi
BW Reporters
